CAPEC-150 (Collect Data from Common Resource Locations): An adversary exploits well-known locations for resources for the purposes of undermining the security of the target. In many, if not most systems, files and resources are organized in a default tree structure. plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes connected to the Weakness node representing CWE-522 via the EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship. Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its TaxonomyEntry nodes via MAPS_TO where the taxonomy is ATT&CK, to obtain the corresponding ATT&CK technique/sub-technique IDs (entry_id).
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its Mitigation nodes via HAS_MITIGATION to list CAPEC-level countermeasures.

For the ATT&CK technique/sub-technique IDs obtained from q2 (via the attack-technique-id join), retrieve the corresponding Technique and SubTechnique nodes, and for each, retrieve Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

g.V().hasLabel("Weakness").has("id", within(cweIds)).as("w").in("EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").project("w","ap","tax").by(__.select("w").elementMap()).by(__.select("ap").elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes connected via EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS to the Weakness node representing CWE-287. For each matching AttackPattern, retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes (filter to taxonomy ATT&CK) and its HAS_MITIGATION Mitigation nodes.

For the ATT&CK technique and sub-technique IDs resolved from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings (join on attack-technique-id), retrieve the Technique and SubTechnique nodes and all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

g.V().hasLabel("Weakness").has("id", within(cweIds)).as("w").in("EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").project("w","ap","tax").by(__.select("w").elementMap()).by(__.select("ap").elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation): Adversaries may abuse Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute malicious commands and payloads. WMI is designed for programmers and is the infrastructure for management data and operations on Windows systems.(Citation: WMI 1-3) WMI is an administration feature that provides a uniform environment to access Windows system components.

T1059.001 (PowerShell) has revoked: False; stix_type: attack-pattern; x_mitre_deprecated: False; x_mitre_is_subtechnique: True; x_mitre_remote_support: False; x_mitre_version: 1.5; x_mitre_contributors: Mayuresh Dani, Qualys Praetorian Ross Brittain; x_mitre_domains: enterprise-attack; x_mitre_platforms: Windows.

T1059.001 (PowerShell): Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system.(Citation: TechNet PowerShell) Adversaries can use PowerShell to perform a number of actions, including discovery of information and execution of code. Examples include the Start-Process cmdlet which can be used to run an executable and the Invoke-Command cmdlet which runs a command locally or on a remote computer (though administrator permissions are required to use PowerShell to connect to remote systems).
T1059.003 (Windows Command Shell) attack id: T1059.003.

T1059.003 (Windows Command Shell) has revoked: False; stix_type: attack-pattern; x_mitre_deprecated: False; x_mitre_is_subtechnique: True; x_mitre_remote_support: False; x_mitre_version: 1.5; x_mitre_domains: enterprise-attack; x_mitre_platforms: Windows.

T1059.003 (Windows Command Shell): Adversaries may abuse the Windows command shell for execution. The Windows command shell (cmd) is the primary command prompt on Windows systems. The Windows command prompt can be used to control almost any aspect of a system, with various permission levels required for different subsets of commands. The command prompt can be invoked remotely via Remote Services such as SSH.(Citation: SSH in Windows)

Batch files (ex: .bat or .cmd) also provide the shell with a list of sequential commands to run, as well as normal scripting operations such as conditionals and loops. Common uses of batch files include long or repetitive tasks, or the need to run the same set of commands on multiple systems.

plan.text: Find the Software that is the built-in Windows interface for administrative scripting and management (e.g., PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation, or Windows Command Shell), and identify the DataComponents (assets) it targets or is associated with via its Techniques and DetectionStrategies.

queries: MATCH (n) WHERE (n:Analytic OR n:Campaign OR n:DataComponent OR n:DetectionStrategy OR n:Group OR n:Matrix OR n:Mitigation OR n:Software OR n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) AND any(term IN $names WHERE toLower(n.name) CONTAINS term) WITH collect(n) AS cand WITH cand, [x IN cand WHERE any(t IN $names WHERE toLower(x.name) = t)] AS exact UNWIND (CASE WHEN size(exact) > 0 THEN exact ELSE cand END) AS n OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

plan.text: Identify the Technique or SubTechnique corresponding to the native Windows administration interface designed for programmers to run commands and manage operations across a system (e.g., Windows Command Shell / Command Prompt / cmd.exe). Retrieve the matching Technique node, its parent Tactic, and any child SubTechniques.

For the technique identified in q1, retrieve all DataComponents that are MONITORSed by Analytics belonging to DetectionStrategies that DETECT that technique. This code can allow them to maintain persistence or move laterally within an enclave because it is executed every time the affected user or users logon to a computer. CAPEC-564 (Run Software at Logon) has Abstraction: Detailed; Status: Draft.

CAPEC-564 (Run Software at Logon): Operating system allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or users logon to a system. If adversaries can access these scripts, they may insert additional code into the logon script. This code can allow them to maintain persistence or move laterally within an enclave because it is executed every time the affected user or users logon to a computer. Modifying logon scripts can effectively bypass workstation and enclave firewalls. Depending on the access configuration of the logon scripts, either local credentials or a remote administrative account may be necessary.

queries: MATCH (n:SubTechnique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

T1550.002 (Pass the Hash): Adversaries may “pass the hash” using stolen password hashes to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls. Pass the hash (PtH) is a method of authenticating as a user without having access to the user's cleartext password. This method bypasses standard authentication steps that require a cleartext password, moving directly into the portion of the authentication that uses the password hash.

When performing PtH, valid password hashes for the account being used are captured using a Credential Access technique. Captured hashes are used with PtH to authenticate as that user. Once authenticated, PtH may be used to perform actions on local or remote systems.

queries: MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().has("id", within(ids)).project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

CAPEC-565 (Password Spraying) has Abstraction: Detailed; Likelihood_Of_Attack: High; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: High.

CAPEC-565 (Password Spraying): In a Password Spraying attack, an adversary tries a small list (e.g. 3-5) of common or expected passwords, often matching the target's complexity policy, against a known list of user accounts to gain valid credentials. The adversary tries a particular password for each user account, before moving onto the next password in the list. This approach assists the adversary in remaining undetected by avoiding rapid or frequent account lockouts. The adversary may then reattempt the process with additional passwords, once enough time has passed to prevent inducing a lockout.

gold_question: Which ATT&CK tactics do the techniques mapped from CAPEC-633 (Token Impersonation) belong to?
note: swapped tactics/techniques/mapped/belong for plain phrasing; kept CAPEC-633

plan.text: Find the AttackPattern with CAPEC id 633 and retrieve its TaxonomyEntry mapping to the ATT&CK taxonomy (MAPS_TO where taxonomy_name = 'ATTACK'), returning the mapped entry_id (ATT&CK technique id).

For the ATT&CK technique/sub-technique id(s) obtained from the CAPEC-633 mapping, retrieve the Technique or SubTechnique node and traverse HAS_TACTIC to return all associated Tactic nodes (the high-level attack goals).

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

Return the AttackPattern name, ID, and the linking TaxonomyEntry.

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes connected via EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS to the Weakness node representing CWE-287 (Improper Authentication). Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.

For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its TaxonomyEntry nodes reachable via MAPS_TO where the taxonomy is ATT&CK, to obtain the corresponding ATT&CK technique/sub-technique IDs (entry_id).
Retrieve Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK IDs obtained from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings in q2. Return technique names, IDs, and parent tactic.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION. Return mitigation descriptions and any associated resources or skills.
For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q3, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES. Return mitigation names, IDs, and descriptions.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t:Technique) RETURN ta.attack_id AS tactic_id, ta.name AS tactic_name, t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

g.V().hasLabel("Weakness").has("id", within(cweIds)).as("w").in("EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").project("w","ap","tax").by(__.select("w").elementMap()).by(__.select("ap").elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

note: schema words replaced with plain phrasing

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to the Weakness node representing CWE-294. Return the AttackPattern id, name, and description.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes where the taxonomy_name is 'ATTACK', returning the entry_id (ATT&CK technique id) and any mapping notes.
Retrieve the Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK ids obtained from q2. Return technique name, description, and tactic associations.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes linked via HAS_MITIGATION. Return mitigation name and description.
For the Technique and SubTechnique nodes resolved in q3, retrieve all Mitigation nodes that have a MITIGATES relationship to them. Return mitigation name and description.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t:Technique) RETURN ta.attack_id AS tactic_id, ta.name AS tactic_name, t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

gold_question: Which CAPEC patterns exploit weakness CWE-308, which ATT&CK techniques do they map to, and what mitigations apply?
note: dash-fragment sentence shape

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to the Weakness node representing CWE-308 (Improper Handling of Case Sensitivity). Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.

For each AttackPattern identified in q1 (exploiting CWE-308), find its TaxonomyEntry nodes via MAPS_TO where taxonomy_name is 'ATTACK'. Return the entry_id values (ATT&CK technique IDs) for each pattern.
Find all Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK IDs obtained from q2. Return their names, IDs, and parent tactic where applicable.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1 (exploiting CWE-308), find all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION. Return mitigation descriptions and any associated resources or skills.
For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q3, find all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES. Return mitigation names, IDs, and descriptions.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000

CAPEC-66 (SQL Injection) has 3 mitigations, named only as text: “Strong input validation - All user-controllable input must be validated and filtered for illegal characters as well as SQL content. Keywords such as UNION, SELECT or INSERT must be filtered in addition to characters such as a single-quote(') or SQL-comments (--) based on the context in which they appear.”; “Use of parameterized queries or stored procedures - Parameterization causes the input to be restricted to certain domains, such as strings or integers, and any input outside such domains is considered invalid and the query fails. Note that SQL Injection is possible even in the presence of stored procedures if the eventual query is constructed dynamically.”; “Use of custom error pages - Attackers can glean information about the nature of queries from descriptive error messages. Input validation must be coupled with customized error pages that inform about an error without disclosing information about the database or application.”.

CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters) has Abstraction: Detailed; Likelihood_Of_Attack: Medium; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: Medium.

CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters): Some APIs will strip certain leading characters from a string of parameters. An adversary can intentionally introduce leading "ghost" characters (extra characters that don't affect the validity of the request at the API layer) that enable the input to pass the filters and therefore process the adversary's input. This occurs when the targeted API will accept input data in several syntactic forms and interpret it in the equivalent semantic way, while the filter does not take into account the full spectrum of the syntactic forms acceptable to the targeted API.

CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters) has 3 mitigations, named only as text: “Use an allowlist rather than a denylist input validation.”; “Canonicalize all data prior to validation.”; “Take an iterative approach to input validation (defense in depth).”.
CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters) has Abstraction: Detailed; Likelihood_Of_Attack: Medium; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: Medium.

CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters): Some APIs will strip certain leading characters from a string of parameters. An adversary can intentionally introduce leading "ghost" characters (extra characters that don't affect the validity of the request at the API layer) that enable the input to pass the filters and therefore process the adversary's input. This occurs when the targeted API will accept input data in several syntactic forms and interpret it in the equivalent semantic way, while the filter does not take into account the full spectrum of the syntactic forms acceptable to the targeted API.

plan.text: Find the AttackPattern whose name is 'XSS Targeting Non-Script Elements' and follow its MAPS_TO relationship to TaxonomyEntry nodes where taxonomy_name is 'ATTACK' to retrieve the mapped ATT&CK technique IDs.

For the Technique and SubTechnique nodes identified in q2, retrieve all connected Mitigation nodes via the MITIGATES relationship to list applicable defensive measures.
For the AttackPattern 'XSS Targeting Non-Script Elements', retrieve all connected Mitigation nodes via the HAS_MITIGATION relationship to list CAPEC-level countermeasures.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

claims: CAPEC-63 (Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)) has 5 ExecutionSteps, named only as text: “Explore 1 [Survey the application for user-controllable inputs] Using a browser or an automated tool, an attacker follows all public links and actions on a web site. They record all the links, the forms, the resources accessed and all other potential entry-points for the web application.”; “Experiment 2 [Probe identified potential entry points for XSS vulnerability] The attacker uses the entry points gathered in the "Explore" phase as a target list and injects various common script payloads to determine if an entry point actually represents a vulnerability and to characterize the extent to which the vulnerability can be exploited.”; “Exploit 3 [Steal session IDs, credentials, page content, etc.] As the attacker succeeds in exploiting the vulnerability, they can choose to steal user's credentials in order to reuse or to analyze them later on.”; “Exploit 4 [Forceful browsing] When the attacker targets the current application or another one (through CSRF vulnerabilities), the user will then be the one who perform the attacks without being aware of it. These attacks are mostly targeting application logic flaws, but it can also be used to create a widespread attack against a particular website on the user's current network (Internet or not).”; “Exploit 5 [Content spoofing] By manipulating the content, the attacker targets the information that the user would like to get from the website.”.

CAPEC-63 (Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)) has 8 mitigations, named only as text: “Design: Use browser technologies that do not allow client side scripting.”; “Design: Utilize strict type, character, and encoding enforcement”; “Design: Server side developers should not proxy content via XHR or other means, if a http proxy for remote content is setup on the server side, the client's browser has no way of discerning where the data is originating from.”; “Implementation: Ensure all content that is delivered to client is sanitized against an acceptable content specification.”; “Implementation: Perform input validation for all remote content.”; “Implementation: Perform output validation for all remote content.”; “Implementation: Session tokens for specific host”; “Implementation: Patching software. There are many attack vectors for XSS on the client side and the server side. Many vulnerabilities are fixed in service packs for browser, web servers, and plug in technologies, staying current on patch release that deal with XSS countermeasures mitigates this.”.
CAPEC-63 (Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)) has Abstraction: Standard; Likelihood_Of_Attack: High; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: Very High.

CAPEC-63 (Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)): An adversary embeds malicious scripts in content that will be served to web browsers. The goal of the attack is for the target software, the client-side browser, to execute the script with the users' privilege level. An attack of this type exploits a programs' vulnerabilities that are brought on by allowing remote hosts to execute code and scripts. Web browsers, for example, have some simple security controls in place, but if a remote attacker is allowed to execute scripts (through injecting them in to user-generated content like bulletin boards) then these controls may be bypassed. Further, these attacks are very difficult for an end user to detect.

plan.text: Find the AttackPatterns named 'Embedding Scripts within Scripts', 'Leverage Executable Code in Non-Executable Files', and 'Embed Virus into DLL'; for each, follow MAPS_TO to TaxonomyEntry nodes where taxonomy_name = 'ATTACK' and return the entry_id (ATT&CK technique/sub-technique id) for each mapping.

For the deduplicated set of ATT&CK technique/sub-technique ids obtained from q1 (via the attack-technique-id join), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES to those Technique or SubTechnique nodes, returning the mitigation id, name, and the technique id it mitigates.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
question: Which ATT&CK techniques do Embedding Scripts within Scripts, Leverage Executable Code in Non-Executable Files, and Embed Virus into DLL map to (they overlap), and what mitigations apply to the deduplicated union?

Return the technique/sub-technique IDs and names for each behavior.", query='MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000')

gold_question: Which ATT&CK techniques do CAPEC-19, CAPEC-35, CAPEC-448 map to (they overlap), and what mitigations apply to the deduplicated union?
note: paraphrased all three names' ideas, no identifiers/names/avoid words

plan.text: Identify the Technique and SubTechnique nodes that correspond to each of three described adversary behaviors: (1) embedding one script inside another so it executes covertly (script insertion / obfuscated scripting), (2) inserting runnable code into file formats not intended to execute code such as images or configuration files (embedded masquerading in non-executable containers), and (3) hiding malicious code in unused padding bytes within a compiled library's instruction stream (code concealment in binary padding). Return the technique/sub-technique IDs and names for each behavior.

For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship, to assemble the combined set of ATT&CK countermeasures that address all three behaviors together.

Find AttackPattern nodes that have a MAPS_TO relationship to a TaxonomyEntry whose taxonomy_name is 'ATTACK' (i.e., CAPEC patterns formally mapped to ATT&CK techniques), and for each such AttackPattern retrieve its associated Mitigation nodes via HAS_MITIGATION. This yields complementary countermeasures from the CAPEC perspective for the same adversary behaviors.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
question: Since these three approaches overlap — hiding one script inside another so it quietly runs too, sneaking runnable code into files that aren't meant to run any code themselves (like an image or configuration file), and slipping a virus into leftover padding inside a compiled library's instructions — which adversary behaviors would each line up with, and what combined set of countermeasures would help?

plan.text: Identify the three CAPEC attack patterns matching these descriptions: (1) a script hidden inside another script that a target program is likely to execute, enabled by a remote-code-execution flaw; (2) exploitation of a system's trust in its own configuration or resource files so that loading an altered image or settings file causes hidden code to run or the running process to be hijacked; (3) tampering with a compiled library by planting a virus in the padding gaps left between legitimate instructions by compiler optimizations, infecting any later consumer of that library. For each pattern, retrieve its ExecutionSteps, Prerequisites, Resources, Skills, Weaknesses, Indicators, Consequences, and Mitigations.

Retrieve the ATT&CK Techniques and SubTechniques (with their parent Tactic) that correspond to the three CAPEC attack patterns identified in q1, as linked via the declared attack-technique-id join (CAPEC TaxonomyEntry with taxonomy_name=ATTACK mapping to Technique/SubTechnique attack_id).

For the ATT&CK Techniques and SubTechniques identified in q2, retrieve all associated Mitigations (defensive measures that reduce technique risk) and any DetectionStrategies and Analytics that monitor for those techniques.

For the three CAPEC attack patterns identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigations, Prerequisites, Resources, and Skills associated with each pattern, to complement the ATT&CK-side countermeasures and form a combined set of defensive recommendations.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000

For each ATT&CK technique/sub-technique ID received via the attack-technique-id join, retrieve the matching Technique or SubTechnique node and all Mitigation nodes reachable via the MITIGATES relationship; return the full set so the union can be deduplicated.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

gold_question: Which ATT&CK techniques do CAPEC-13, CAPEC-640 map to (they overlap), and what mitigations apply to the deduplicated union?
note: paraphrased both names' ideas, no identifiers/names/avoid words

plan.text: Find the Technique or SubTechnique that matches 'quietly changing the environment settings a program depends on so it behaves in the adversary's favor' (e.g., environment variable manipulation, execution-flow hijacking via environment, or registry/configuration modification that alters program behavior). Return the technique name, ID, and all Mitigations linked via MITIGATES.

Find the Technique or SubTechnique that matches 'slipping outside code into the memory space of an already-running, separate process by taking advantage of a program's failure to check that process's integrity' (e.g., Process Injection, Process Hollowing, or Dynamic Code Loading into another process). Return the technique name, ID, and all Mitigations linked via MITIGATES.

Find the AttackPattern that matches 'modifying or manipulating environment settings, configuration, or runtime parameters that a target program depends on, causing it to behave in the attacker's favor'. Return the pattern name, ID, and all Mitigations linked via HAS_MITIGATION.

Find the AttackPattern that matches 'injecting or loading code into the memory space of an already-running, separate process, exploiting the target's failure to validate the integrity of its own process memory'. Return the pattern name, ID, and all Mitigations linked via HAS_MITIGATION.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

question: Since these two approaches overlap — quietly changing the environment settings a program depends on so it behaves in the adversary's favor, and slipping outside code into the memory space of an already-running, separate process by taking advantage of a program's failure to check that process's integrity — which adversary behaviors would each line up with, and what combined set of countermeasures would help?

plan.text: Find the Technique or SubTechnique that describes an adversary modifying environment variables or environment settings that a running program reads, causing the program to deviate from its intended behavior and act in favor of the modifier. Retrieve the matching Technique/SubTechnique node(s) and all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES.

Find the Technique or SubTechnique that describes an adversary exploiting a program's failure to re-verify that a separate, already-running process is still legitimate, then injecting external instructions or code into that process's own memory space, potentially reaching resources within reach. Retrieve the matching Technique/SubTechnique node(s) and all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES.

Find the AttackPattern(s) that describe an adversary modifying environment variables, configuration files, or runtime settings that a running program reads, causing the program to behave in a way that favors the attacker rather than its intended purpose. Retrieve the matching AttackPattern node(s) and all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION.

Find the AttackPattern(s) that describe an adversary injecting external code or instructions into a separate, already-running process's memory space by exploiting the program's trust in or failure to re-verify that process's legitimacy, potentially gaining access to resources within that process's reach. Retrieve the matching AttackPattern node(s) and all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION.

Find Techniques and SubTechniques that describe an adversary searching through files an application left without proper access controls to find sensitive information hidden inside them (e.g., Data from Local System, Data from Network Shared Drive, Data from Information Repositories, Data from Cloud Storage). Return the technique name, ID, and tactic.

For the Techniques and SubTechniques identified in q1 and q2, retrieve all Mitigations connected via the MITIGATES relationship. Return mitigation name, ID, and the technique(s) each mitigates, so the combined (union) set of countermeasures covering both approaches can be assembled.

Find AttackPatterns whose MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry has taxonomy_name='ATTACK' and an entry_id matching any of the ATT&CK technique/sub-technique IDs returned by q1 and q2. For each matching AttackPattern, also retrieve its Mitigations via HAS_MITIGATION and its Consequences via HAS_CONSEQUENCE. Return the CAPEC pattern name, ID, mapped ATT&CK ID, mitigations, and consequences.

gold_question: Which ATT&CK techniques do CAPEC-37, CAPEC-639 map to (they overlap), and what mitigations apply to the deduplicated union?
note: built from both descriptions only, no identifiers/names/avoid words

plan.text: Identify the Technique (and any child SubTechniques) that describes an adversary carefully inspecting a system for confidential details — account numbers, keys, credentials — that were left embedded in the system and are valuable as a stepping stone toward further access or privilege escalation.

Identify the Technique (and any child SubTechniques) that describes an adversary simply opening and reading files that an application left without proper access controls, looking for sensitive information that was never meant to be exposed.

Retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES to the techniques identified in q1 (unsecured-credentials inspection) and q2 (reading files without access controls), so the combined countermeasure set can be assembled.

Find AttackPatterns that MAPS_TO a TaxonomyEntry with taxonomy_name='ATTACK' whose entry_id matches the ATT&CK technique IDs resolved in q1 and q2; for each matching AttackPattern, retrieve its Mitigations via HAS_MITIGATION to supplement the combined countermeasure set.

queries: MATCH (n:SubTechnique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 50
MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 50

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 200

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(200)
question: Picture two separate tricks that overlap here: one carefully inspects a system looking for confidential details — account numbers, keys, credentials — that were left embedded inside it, valuable as a stepping stone toward a bigger goal; the other simply opens up files an application left without proper access controls and reads through them looking for whatever sensitive information was never meant to be exposed — which adversary behaviors would each line up with, and what combined set of countermeasures would help?
